sentences.text: Mapusaurus looked like Giganotosaurus but had a deeper and narrower skull with a rougher upper jaw bone.
Its lacrimal bone was textured and the second neck vertebra featured a neural spine that was longer and more slender than in related forms.
Fossils include parts of the skull, teeth, vertebrae, pelvis, ribs, hindlimbs, foot bones, and forelimb fragments, noting that the shoulder blade and coracoid stayed separate rather than fusing.

The largest known specimen, identified by a left femur, was originally estimated at 10.2 meters long and weighing 3 tons, though later studies revised the maximum size to between 10.2 and 12.6 meters and 6 to 8 tons in mass.
This bonebed may provide the first substantive evidence of gregarious behavior in large theropods, though it is unknown if they hunted in organized packs or as a mob.

The first fossils were discovered in 1997 at Cañadón del Gato, located 20 km south of Plaza Huincul in Neuquén Province, Argentina, and were excavated between 1997 and 2001 by the Argentine-Canadian Proyecto Dinosaurio expedition.
These fossils were found in a bonebed containing seven to nine individuals of various growth stages.
The remains were found in the Lower Cretaceous Huincul Formation, which consists of fine-to-medium grain sandstones.

A cervical vertebra suffered from an infection possibly similar to tuberculosis, while two ribs were fractured and rehealed, likely belonging to an older individual. Healed fractures indicate that Mapusaurus lived a hazardous and active lifestyle similar to many theropods. Only 2.8% of Mapusaurus fossils bore pathologies, representing just 11.1% of the total individuals. Analysis suggests that none of the observed diseases caused the death of the individuals in the bonebed.
The genus Mapusaurus was named by Coria and Currie in 2006.

Mapusaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period in Argentina. Mapusaurus coexisted with giant titanosaurs like Argentinosaurus and Choconsaurus, along with rebbachisaurids, unenlagiids, and ceratosaurs. The subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae was likely restricted to the southern continent of Gondwana, where they were probably the apex predators.
Some researchers have suggested that Taurovenator is a synonym of Mapusaurus because they found no unique distinguishing traits in the Taurovenator holotype.

Researchers speculated that the bonebed might represent a predator trap or a coincidental accumulation of carcasses, though this remains a hypothesis. It remains debated whether Mapusaurus hunted in organized groups or simply attacked in bands, as the specific hunting mechanism is unknown.
